extracted.intended_audience: filmmakers/creators and fans interested in submitting or understanding Channel 101 (short pilot festival)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and operational rules for submitting, screening, and continuing short films made in the format of TV pilots at the Channel 101 festival. Covers format, selection, voting, prime-time status, and related procedural constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format — pilot under five minutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants submit a short film in the format of a pilot under five minutes in length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Channel 101 was established as a monthly short film festival with a five-minute format; all screenings start off as episode '101' of their series. Running over five minutes can disqualify a show from continuing (see 'overrunning disqualification').

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission eligibility — open submissions (can be submitted from anywhere)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shows can be submitted from anywhere; festival is based in Los Angeles (with a sister festival in New York City).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the event is held in Los Angeles, the Channel 101 page notes 'shows can be submitted from anywhere', indicating open geographic eligibility for creators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection for screening — panel of previous successful submitters
rubrics_metrics.description: A panel of previously successful submitters chooses what pilots are shown at each screening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The panel selects which pilots will be screened alongside established prime-time shows; prime-time directors later join this panel (see 'prime time benefits'). This is the gatekeeping mechanism that determines what gets shown to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screening programme size — usually ten shorts per screening
rubrics_metrics.description: Roughly once a month the screening features usually ten shorts being screened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because only a limited number of slots are available, the panel must reject additional submissions for time constraints; the festival deliberately limits the programme to around ten shorts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience voting determines continuation
rubrics_metrics.description: A live audience at the screening decides which pilots continue as a series for the next screening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The audience votes on which pilots they would like to see return; this functions like TV ratings, with the audience acting as network executives ('You run the network'). Audience choice, not only panel selection, governs which shows continue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prime time/top five rule — top five make follow-up episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: The top five shows (by audience vote) are entered into the 'prime time' slots on the Channel 101 website and get to make a follow-up episode for the next screening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prime time status permits a show to produce the next episode and confers influence: prime-time directors are part of the panel that decides which five new pilots will be shown alongside established shows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation and cancellation dynamic — series continues until it fails to make top five
rubrics_metrics.description: Series continue with new 'episodes' shown at each screening until one fails to make the top five, at which point the series is cancelled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This replicates TV-series lifecycle dynamics: continued audience approval keeps a series alive; failure to make the top five triggers cancellation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failed/rejected pilots terminology and consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Shows that fail to make the prime time spot are known as 'failed pilots'; shows that fail to make the screenings are known as 'rejected pilots'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failed pilots do not get the prime-time follow-up episode; rejected pilots never make the screening programme. These labels indicate different stages of non-selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overrunning disqualification (voluntary cancellation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some successful shows can choose to be cancelled voluntarily by running over five minutes in length, disqualifying the show from continuing and leaving one last un-voted episode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceeding the five-minute limit is an explicit mechanism creators have used to voluntarily end a series; it is treated as disqualifying for continuation under Channel 101 rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chauncey rule (historical exception allowing forced screening)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Chauncey' rule (introduced Oct 2003, removed Nov 2005) allowed a director to overrule the voting panel and force their pilot to be screened, but the audience retained the option of stopping the film at any time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Chauncey was an honor-system exception named after Chris Chauncey; it was retired as the festival grew because the honor system became unworkable. Only one Chauncey-made show reached prime time (Dick Richards: Private Dick).

rubrics_metrics.name: Season structure — ten screenings per calendar year
rubrics_metrics.description: Each calendar year of the festival is referred to as a 'season', comprising 10 screenings due to there being no December screening and a month break between spring/summer and November (the awards show).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The November screening is the yearly awards show ('Channy'). This schedule affects production cadence and when follow-up episodes will be screened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prime-time directors' privilege — panel membership and programming influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Prime-time directors are part of the panel that decides which five new pilots will be shown alongside the five established shows from the previous screening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achieving prime time confers both continued screening and influence over future screening selections, creating an incentive structure for creators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/compliance risk — shows can be removed after legal challenge
rubrics_metrics.description: A show can be cancelled or removed from the Channel 101 site following legal action (example: House of Cosbys was cancelled and removed after a cease and desist letter from Cosby's lawyers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creators must be aware of copyright and rights clearance risks; legal complaints can lead to removal irrespective of audience or panel success.
